title: PathResourceResolver.checkResource relies on string prefix comparison of resource paths that are only partially normalized
decision_reason: Discusses PathResourceResolver rather than the benchmark's ResourceServlet path-normalization fix; a separate concern is not credited as the designated target.
candidate_description: In `isResourceUnderLocation` (PathResourceResolver), the resource path and the location path are compared with `startsWith` after only the LOCATION side (and, for ClassPathResource/ServletContextResource, both sides via `getPath()`) has been passed through `StringUtils.cleanPath`. For `UrlResource` the resource path is taken raw from `resource.getURL().toExternalForm()` (line 169) while the location is cleaned (line 170). The trailing guard only inspects the already-read-only resolved resource path for the literal substring `../` after a single `URLDecoder.decode`. This is a prefix-check-based containment test, which is the weakest form of path containment validation: any input whose cleaned form still yields a readable resource under the location but whose string form is not a true descendant passes, and the guard does not compare canonical/normalized filesystem paths (e.g. via `getCanonicalPath`) nor reject alternate separators or encoded traversal sequences that survive one decode pass. This is a candidate guard weakness whose exploitability depends on how the container and `location.createRelative` handle the request path; I could not demonstrate a concrete bypass from source alone.
ground_truth_root_cause: ResourceServlet includes a caller-provided resource path without first normalizing it; the fix applies StringUtils.cleanPath before allow-pattern checking and RequestDispatcher.include.
ground_truth_note: The target is the ResourceServlet path normalization defect. A candidate about PathResourceResolver is a different implementation/path and is not credited for this target.

title: ResourceServlet includes a request-parameter-controlled resource path when allowedResources is not configured
decision_reason: Identifies ResourceServlet's raw request-parameter path reaching RequestDispatcher.include without normalization; the reference fix applies cleanPath before checking and including that path.
candidate_description: `ResourceServlet.determineResourceUrl` returns the raw value of the request parameter named `resource` (line 240-242). `doGet` passes that value to `doInclude`, which tokenizes it and calls `request.getRequestDispatcher(url).include(request, response)` for each token (lines 277-289). The only restriction applied is the optional Ant-style pattern `allowedResources`; if that property is left at its default `null`, ANY resource path supplied by the caller is included, including paths under `WEB-INF`, as the class javadoc itself states ("If not set, any target resource can be requested, including resources in the WEB-INF directory!", lines 53-56). This is a default-open configuration combined with a RequestDispatcher include of an attacker-supplied path, which is a candidate for resource disclosure / internal-path inclusion. The class is marked `@Deprecated` as of 4.3.5 in favor of `ResourceHttpRequestHandler`, which lowers its practical impact on current deployments.
ground_truth_root_cause: ResourceServlet includes a caller-provided resource path without first normalizing it; the fix applies StringUtils.cleanPath before allow-pattern checking and RequestDispatcher.include.
ground_truth_note: The target is the ResourceServlet path normalization defect. A candidate about PathResourceResolver is a different implementation/path and is not credited for this target.

title: Encoded-path traversal check in PathResourceResolver.isInvalidEncodedPath is substring-based (over-broad ".." match) rather than separator-aware, and is only consulted inside isResourceUnderLocation
decision_reason: Does not identify predictable multipart-boundary generation/content pollution; path-normalization or STOMP/SpEL concerns are different targets.
candidate_description: In spring-webmvc PathResourceResolver, the guard against encoded directory traversal is implemented in isInvalidEncodedPath(String resourcePath): it URL-decodes the resolved resource path and then does decodedPath.indexOf("..") + 2, checks that the character at that offset is '/' or '\\', and then returns true unconditionally for any decoded path that contains ".." at an offset within bounds. Two observations worth flagging: (1) the "return true" is executed for any occurrence of ".." (not only when the char after it is a separator), so the check is intentionally/erroneously broad (it also rejects benign names like "..foo"); this direction of error is fail-closed and therefore not itself a traversal weakness. (2) The check is invoked only from isResourceUnderLocation (line 248), i.e. after the resolved Resource has already been compared against the location's own path prefix; getResource(String,Resource) at lines 179-193 relies on checkResource/isResourceUnderLocation for containment instead of a prefix check applied directly to the request path. If a location (or allowed location) were itself misconfigured as the filesystem root or a path whose prefix check is satisfied, the containment test would not add protection; the encoded-path check would still be the only decoded-traversal filter. I did not find a concrete request path that bypasses the location containment check in this code, so this is recorded as a hardening/robustness observation with the root cause being the substring-style ".." detection and its single call site, not a demonstrated traversal.
ground_truth_root_cause: Multipart request boundaries were insufficiently unpredictable, enabling multipart content pollution when an attacker can guess the boundary; the fix uses SecureRandom for boundary generation.
ground_truth_note: The dataset's failing test name mentions MimeType, but the assigned CVE and patch target multipart boundary predictability/content pollution. Path-normalization and STOMP/SpEL candidates do not match it.

title: Subscription "selector" header is parsed and evaluated as a SpEL expression against message headers (feature-gated, destination-scoped)
decision_reason: Does not identify predictable multipart-boundary generation/content pollution; path-normalization or STOMP/SpEL concerns are different targets.
candidate_description: DefaultSubscriptionRegistry stores an in-memory ExpressionParser (SpelExpressionParser) and, in addSubscriptionInternal (lines 139-161), reads the first native header named by selectorHeaderName (default "selector") off the subscription message, then calls this.expressionParser.parseExpression(selector) and keeps the resulting Expression as the subscription filter. Later, filterSubscriptions evaluates that expression against an EvaluationContext built from message headers. Implications worth documenting: the expression text is client-supplied on a SUBSCRIBE frame (subject to the application's configured selectorHeaderName and to broker configuration), Spring EL is a powerful language, and parsing is guarded by a Throwable catch that only logs. I did not trace whether the evaluation context exposes any type/method references that would make expression evaluation dangerous, so this is reported as a data-flow observation rather than a confirmed issue; the parse step alone does not execute the expression.
ground_truth_root_cause: Multipart request boundaries were insufficiently unpredictable, enabling multipart content pollution when an attacker can guess the boundary; the fix uses SecureRandom for boundary generation.
ground_truth_note: The dataset's failing test name mentions MimeType, but the assigned CVE and patch target multipart boundary predictability/content pollution. Path-normalization and STOMP/SpEL candidates do not match it.

title: Descriptor UI entry points (doAutoCompleteJob / doCheckJob / doCheckWait / newInstance) rely on external authorization not verifiable from this module
decision_reason: Raises a related authorization concern at descriptor UI methods, but does not identify the missing Item.BUILD check in BuildTriggerStepExecution.start; it instead treats the downstream execution path as protected. Related topic, not the benchmark target hit.
candidate_description: BuildTriggerStep.DescriptorImpl exposes Stapler-reachable methods that consume request data: doAutoCompleteJob enumerates item names (filtered by i.hasPermission(Item.READ) at line 151) across the passed ItemGroup; doCheckJob/doCheckWait resolve a caller-supplied job name via Jenkins.getActiveInstance().getItem(value, context, Item.class) and reflect existence/type in the returned FormValidation; newInstance(StaplerRequest req, JSONObject formData) reads formData's "parameter" array, looks up the referenced job with the StaplerReferer-derived context, and for each entry calls ParameterDefinition.createValue(req, jo). These are ordinary Jenkins DataBound/check/autocomplete endpoints whose access control is expected to be enforced by Stapler's Requester/ACL layer and by Jenkins' job-configuration permission checks for the surrounding build-step form. Within this repository there is no explicit permission assertion guarding these methods, and the repository does not include the calling Jelly/UI or Stapler configuration, so the effective guard cannot be confirmed from the reviewed source alone. The runtime scheduling path (step execution) is separately protected by the Item.BUILD permission enforced during queue scheduling (see BuildTriggerStepTest.permissions, lines 422-441), which reduces but does not by itself demonstrate coverage of the descriptor methods.
ground_truth_root_cause: BuildTriggerStepExecution.start triggers a downstream job without checking Item.BUILD for the build authentication.
ground_truth_note: The used Vul4J CSV has a CVE-year/number error. Its fix commit and failing permission test match Jenkins SECURITY-433 / CVE-2017-1000089, not CVE-2018-1000089 (which belongs to django-anymail). Score against the unambiguous fix/test target and disclose the metadata discrepancy.

title: Reflective quiet-period lookup on task class in BuildTriggerStepExecution.start: NoSuchMethodError path returns no value and ClientErrorException would escape the catch list
decision_reason: Does not identify the missing Item.BUILD authorization check before triggering a downstream job; the reflection/quiet-period robustness observation is a different issue.
candidate_description: When quietPeriod is unset for a non-ParameterizedJob Queue.Task, BuildTriggerStepExecution.start reflectively invokes task.getClass().getMethod("getQuietPeriod") (line 118) and stores the result only if the return type equals int.class (lines 119-121). The catch clauses handle NoSuchMethodException (line 122), IllegalAccessError, IllegalArgumentException and InvocationTargetException (line 124). Two edge behaviors follow: (a) if a class does not declare getQuietPeriod at all, NoSuchMethodException occurs and the code silently falls through with quietPeriod still null, so the Jenkins default quiet period is used (line 128-130) — a benign best-effort outcome; (b) if the method exists but the invocation throws a subclass of java.lang.Error other than IllegalAccessError, or any other Throwable not listed, it would propagate out of start() rather than being logged, and the method's checked-exception outcome for the caller is not visible in this file. This is a robustness/error-handling observation about reflective invocation on an arbitrary class; no attacker-controlled class, deserialization, or value flow into a dangerous sink is demonstrated here, and the reflective target is code already loaded in the Jenkins JVM, not input-selected.
ground_truth_root_cause: BuildTriggerStepExecution.start triggers a downstream job without checking Item.BUILD for the build authentication.
ground_truth_note: The used Vul4J CSV has a CVE-year/number error. Its fix commit and failing permission test match Jenkins SECURITY-433 / CVE-2017-1000089, not CVE-2018-1000089 (which belongs to django-anymail). Score against the unambiguous fix/test target and disclose the metadata discrepancy.

title: Subscription selector header parsed as a raw SpEL expression and evaluated with a StandardEvaluationContext in DefaultSubscriptionRegistry
decision_reason: Does not identify predictable multipart-boundary generation/content pollution; path-normalization or STOMP/SpEL concerns are different targets.
candidate_description: DefaultSubscriptionRegistry allows a subscription message to carry a native header named by getSelectorHeaderName() (default "selector"). In addSubscriptionInternal (line 144) that header value is read and, if non-null, passed directly to this.expressionParser.parseExpression(selector) (line 147) with a plain SpelExpressionParser and no allowlist/sanitization of the expression string. The resulting Expression is stored on the subscription (line 159). Later, filterSubscriptions (lines 188-231) evaluates each stored selector expression with a StandardEvaluationContext built over the incoming message plus a SimpMessageHeaderPropertyAccessor (lines 211-214) and calls expression.getValue(context, boolean.class) (line 216). StandardEvaluationContext is the permissive SpEL evaluation context (it supports type references, constructors and, depending on configured resolvers, method invocation), in contrast to SimpleEvaluationContext, which is the restricted variant intended for untrusted expression input. The root cause is the combination of (a) an untrusted, client-supplied expression string and (b) evaluation under a permissive context. Preconditions/limits visible in source: the selector is taken from a native header of the SUBSCRIBE message, so whether the value is truly attacker-controlled depends on the surrounding STOMP/WebSocket channel and its inbound validation; parsing and evaluation are wrapped in broad try/catch(Throwable) handlers (lines 153-157 and 220-227) that log and continue, which suppresses exceptions but does not itself neutralize an expression that evaluates successfully; and no method/type restrictions are applied to the context. I could not confirm reachability of the client header to this method, nor any concrete impact (data access, side effects), so this is reported as an unconfirmed candidate rather than a demonstrated vulnerability.
ground_truth_root_cause: Multipart request boundaries were insufficiently unpredictable, enabling multipart content pollution when an attacker can guess the boundary; the fix uses SecureRandom for boundary generation.

title: Client-supplied STOMP 'selector' header evaluated as Spring EL expression in DefaultSubscriptionRegistry
decision_reason: Does not identify predictable multipart-boundary generation/content pollution; path-normalization or STOMP/SpEL concerns are different targets.
candidate_description:
DefaultSubscriptionRegistry holds an ExpressionParser backed by SpelExpressionParser (line 76). In addSubscriptionInternal, the value of the client-controlled native header named by selectorHeaderName (default "selector", line 72) is taken from the message headers via SimpMessageHeaderAccessor.getFirstNativeHeader (line 144) and passed without validation to expressionParser.parseExpression(selector) (line 147). The parsed expression is stored on the subscription (line 159) and later evaluated in filterSubscriptions with expression.getValue(context, boolean.class) (line 216) using a StandardEvaluationContext whose root object is the message and where a SimpMessageHeaderPropertyAccessor is registered (lines 212-213). The STOMP header reaches this code unmodified: StompSubProtocolHandler.handleMessageFromClient decodes client WebSocket frames (decoder.decode, line 252) and forwards the resulting Message, including client native headers, through outputChannel.send(message) (line 299); SUBSCRIBE frames are recognized as StompCommand.SUBSCRIBE (line 312) and are not stripped of the selector native header in the read range. Because SpEL with StandardEvaluationContext permits method invocation and type references by default, a STOMP client that can open a subscription could supply a selector such as a type-reference/method-invocation expression, yielding expression injection beyond simple header comparison; the class javadoc itself states the selector header "can use Spring EL expressions against message headers" (lines 53-55, 113-116).

Evidence of the flow: header value -> parseExpression (no allowlist/regex/sanitization between lines 144-147), expression retained (159), evaluation context built from the message (212-213), evaluated (216). The bounds/try-catch at lines 153-157 and 220-227 only log parse/evaluation failures (logged at debug/trace); they are not input restrictions.

title: HTTP invoker unsafe Java deserialization without class filtering
decision_reason: Discusses PathResourceResolver rather than the benchmark's ResourceServlet path-normalization fix; a separate concern is not credited as the designated target.
candidate_description: RemoteInvocationSerializingExporter.doReadRemoteInvocation calls ObjectInputStream.readObject() directly and only checks the type after the entire object graph has been deserialized. Because ConfigurableObjectInputStream (the base of CodebaseAwareObjectInputStream used here) only controls ClassLoader resolution and proxy-class acceptance, and performs no allow-list/deny-list validation of the classes being deserialized, an attacker who can submit a crafted serialized stream (gadget chain) can trigger arbitrary code execution during deserialization before the RemoteInvocation instanceof check is ever reached. HttpInvokerServiceExporter wires a raw HTTP request input stream directly into this path via readRemoteInvocation -> createObjectInputStream -> doReadRemoteInvocation.

title: STOMP 'selector' header SpEL evaluation with StandardEvaluationContext (expression injection)

title: STOMP subscription selector header evaluated as SpEL with StandardEvaluationContext (remote code execution surface)
decision_reason: Discusses PathResourceResolver rather than the benchmark's ResourceServlet path-normalization fix; a separate concern is not credited as the designated target.
candidate_description: DefaultSubscriptionRegistry reads a 'selector' native header from a client SUBSCRIBE message and passes it to SpelExpressionParser.parseExpression. The resulting Expression is later evaluated in filterSubscriptions using a StandardEvaluationContext whose root object is the incoming Message. StandardEvaluationContext supplies the default reflective property accessor, type references, constructors and method invocation, so a client-controlled selector expression can invoke arbitrary reachable classes/methods (e.g. T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec(...)) rather than being limited to simple header comparisons. The custom SimpMessageHeaderPropertyAccessor only constrains property access on Message/MessageHeaders targets and does not disable reflective access, type references, or method resolution on other objects. The expression is evaluated via expression.getValue(context, boolean.class) in filterSubscriptions when messages match the subscribed destination.

title: STOMP subscription selector header evaluated as SpEL from attacker input
decision_reason: Does not identify denial of service in HttpRange/resource range processing; SpEL and XML-entity concerns are different targets.
candidate_description: The default STOMP simple broker (DefaultSubscriptionRegistry) parses a client-supplied `selector` STOMP header as a SpEL expression and later evaluates it at message-delivery time. The evaluation context is SimpleEvaluationContext with only the custom SimpMessageHeaderPropertyAccessor, intended to block type references, constructors, bean references, and reflective property access. However, the expression is fully attacker-controlled and evaluated on the server. If property/method resolution permitted reaching a dangerous target (e.g., a reflective sink exposed through the message root or the accessor), evaluation could reach security-sensitive operations. Root concern is compiling and executing untrusted expressions from a network peer.
ground_truth_root_cause: Range request processing can be forced into denial of service with a high number of ranges and/or wide overlapping ranges when serving resources.
ground_truth_note: No submitted candidate identifies the HttpRange/Resource range-processing target; unrelated SpEL and XML entity-resolution concerns are not credited.

title: SourceHttpMessageConverter external entity flag enables unguarded XML parsing when enabled
decision_reason: Does not identify denial of service in HttpRange/resource range processing; SpEL and XML-entity concerns are different targets.
candidate_description: SourceHttpMessageConverter reads an HTTP request body into a DOMSource/SAXSource/StAXSource/StreamSource. By default DTD and external entities are disabled. However, the class exposes setProcessExternalEntities(true) (and setSupportDtd(true)) which, when enabled, re-enables external general entities and replaces the no-op entity resolver, thereby permitting XXE/DTD-based SSRF or file read for an application that enables these flags and accepts attacker-controlled XML bodies.

title: DefaultDocumentLoader does not itself disable external entity resolution
decision_reason: Does not identify denial of service in HttpRange/resource range processing; SpEL and XML-entity concerns are different targets.
candidate_description: DefaultDocumentLoader.loadDocument builds a DocumentBuilderFactory and parses an InputSource without setting disallow-doctype-decl or external-general-entities features and without installing an entity resolver of its own. If an application loads untrusted XML with DTD validation through this loader, external entities could be resolved. In standard XmlBeanDefinitionReader usage the caller typically supplies a schema/DTD entity resolver, but entity resolution of general entities is not disabled at this layer.

title: STOMP subscription selector evaluated as SpEL with StandardEvaluationContext (potential RCE)
decision_reason: Does not identify predictable multipart-boundary generation/content pollution; path-normalization or STOMP/SpEL concerns are different targets.
candidate_description: DefaultSubscriptionRegistry reads the 'selector' native header from an inbound SUBSCRIBE message and parses it as a Spring Expression Language expression. When filtering matched subscriptions, the parsed expression is evaluated against an EvaluationContext built as `new StandardEvaluationContext(message)` with a custom property accessor. StandardEvaluationContext enables the full SpEL language subset (type references via T(), constructor references, bean references, method invocation, reflection), so an attacker who can control the selector header can execute arbitrary code reachable via SpEL, e.g. `T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec(...)`. The snapshot still uses the vulnerable StandardEvaluationContext rather than SimpleEvaluationContext (the later 4.3.15 fix for CVE-2018-1270).
